text: Rotate nums to the right by k steps, where k is at least zero. Try to do it in place, with constant extra space.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — for one through seven with k equal to three, I get five, six, seven, one, two, three, four: the last k elements wrap to the front. So if B is the last k elements and A is everything before it, rotating right turns A B into B A. Are there any constraints on the input size — can k be larger than n?
Yes. k can be up to ten to the fifth, possibly larger than n.
Then I normalize with k mod-equals n first. Rotating by a multiple of n changes nothing, and it also keeps my segment bounds inside the array.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would rotate one step at a time, k times — that's n times k, way too slow. There are three standard ways to do better. First, an extra array: each element goes to index i plus k, mod n — simplest, but linear extra space. Second, cyclic replacement: constant space, but fiddly, because there are gcd of n and k separate cycles to follow. This problem reminds me of reversing with converging two pointers: three reversals give constant space and are the cleanest to get right. I'll go with that. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. But why do three reversals produce the rotation?

Because reversing a concatenation X Y gives Y reversed, then X reversed. Reverse the whole array: A B becomes B reversed, then A reversed — B is now up front and A at the back, but each block is backwards. Reverse the first k, and B is fixed; reverse the rest, and A is fixed. The result is B A. The full reverse moves the blocks; the two partial reverses fix their internal order.
Here's the plan. One: take k mod n. Two: reverse the whole array. Three: reverse the first k elements, then reverse the rest. Each reverse is a converging two-pointer: swap the ends, walk inward.

Alright, let me code this up. It's five lines: the size, the modulo, and three calls to the standard reverse — the whole array, then begin to begin plus k, then begin plus k to the end. If the library reverse weren't allowed, each call is just a two-pointer swap loop. One thing worth flagging — the modulo has to come before the reverses. Without it, begin plus k could point past the end of the array, which is undefined behavior. The half-open ranges matter too: the first part is zero up to k, exclusive, and the rest starts exactly at k.

Let's dry-run the code. One through seven, with k equal to three — expected five, six, seven, one, two, three, four. Reversing everything gives seven down to one, and reversing the first three gives five, six, seven up front. The row that matters is the last one: reversing the rest turns four, three, two, one into one, two, three, four. That matches. Corner cases: one, two with k equal to three — k becomes one, giving two, one; without the modulo, begin plus three runs past the end. k equal to zero, or any multiple of n, leaves the array unchanged. A single element is always unchanged.
How would you rotate left instead?
Left by k equals right by n minus k. So I set k to n minus k mod n, all mod n, and reuse the exact same three reversals — a one-line change.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: each element is moved twice across the three reversals. Space is constant — fully in place, just a few index variables. Oh, one more thing — the reversal itself is the classic converging two-pointer: start at both ends, swap, move inward. And a related check, whether one string is a rotation of another, reduces to asking whether it's a substring of the other string doubled, given equal lengths.
Clean — you normalized k, proved the reversal identity, and connected it to the two-pointer primitive. That's a pass.
